content: 1. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA levels are typically very low, often less than 200 IU/mL, in individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Most of these individuals also test positive for anti-HBc antibodies. 2. Treatment failure in CHB can be classified as either primary or secondary. 3. Primary antiviral treatment failure is defined as the inability of an antiviral drug to reduce HBV DNA levels by at least 1 log10 IU/mL within three months of initiating therapy, provided HBV DNA testing is available. 4. Secondary antiviral treatment failure is characterized by a rebound in HBV DNA levels of at least 1 log10 IU/mL from the lowest level (nadir) achieved in individuals who initially responded to treatment with a reduction of at least 1 log10 IU/mL in serum HBV DNA. 5. In settings where HBV DNA testing is unavailable, treatment failure and drug resistance may be suspected based on factors such as the use of antiviral drugs with a low barrier to resistance, poor adherence to therapy, elevated serum aminotransferase levels, and/or evidence of progressive liver disease. 6. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevation tends to occur late and is a relatively poor predictor of drug resistance. 7. ALT and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are intracellular enzymes released into the bloodstream following liver cell injury or death, serving as markers of liver cell damage. 8. HBV DNA represents the viral genome and can be detected and quantified in serum. HBV DNA levels correlate with the amount of circulating viral particles and are measured in IU/mL or copies/mL. To convert copies/mL to IU/mL, divide by 5 (e.g., 10,000 copies/mL = 2,000 IU/mL). 9. An undetectable viral load is defined as an HBV DNA level below the sensitivity threshold of the laboratory assay, typically less than 15 IU/mL for sensitive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays. 10. Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a host cellular protein that may be elevated in individuals with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 11. ALT levels in individuals with CHB often fluctuate and require longitudinal monitoring to determine trends. The upper limit of normal ALT is defined as less than 30 U/L for men and less than 19 U/L for women, though local laboratory reference ranges should be applied. 12. The aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index (APRI) is a simple non-invasive test for estimating hepatic fibrosis. It is calculated using the formula: APRI = [(AST/ULN) x 100] / platelet count (109/L). 13. The FIB-4 index is another non-invasive test for hepatic fibrosis, calculated as: FIB-4 = (age [years] x AST [IU/L]) / (platelet count [109/L] x √ALT [IU/L]). 14. FibroTest (FibroSure) is a commercial biomarker test that uses six blood markers to estimate hepatic fibrosis. 15. Transient elastography (FibroScan) measures liver stiffness as a surrogate for fibrosis by assessing the propagation of a shear wave through the liver. 16. Positive predictive value (PPV) refers to the probability that a positive test result accurately indicates the presence of infection or disease. PPV is influenced by the prevalence of the disease in the population. 17. True negatives (TN) occur when a negative test result correctly identifies the absence of infection or disease. 18. True positives (TP) occur when a positive test result correctly identifies the presence of infection or disease. 19. False negatives (FN) occur when a negative test result fails to identify the presence of infection or disease, often due to assay or test inaccuracies. 20. False positives (FP) occur when a positive test result incorrectly indicates the presence of infection or disease, also often due to assay or test inaccuracies. 21. Hepatitis B infection is caused by HBV, an enveloped DNA virus that infects the liver, leading to hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. 22. HBV infection can be acute or chronic, with associated illnesses ranging from asymptomatic to symptomatic progressive disease. 23. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is defined as the persistence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) for six months or more. It is a significant public health issue, with an estimated 240 million people chronically infected worldwide, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). 24. Major complications of CHB include cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Between 20% and 30% of chronically infected individuals develop these complications, and approximately 650,000 people die annually from CHB-related causes. 25. Many individuals with HBV infection are unaware of their condition and often present with advanced disease. 26. Universal hepatitis B immunization programs targeting infants, with the first dose administered at birth, have been highly effective in reducing the incidence and prevalence of hepatitis B in endemic countries. However, these programs will not significantly impact HBV-related deaths for several decades. 27. Antiviral agents active against HBV can suppress viral replication, prevent progression to cirrhosis, and reduce the risk of HCC and liver-related deaths. However, current treatments do not eradicate the virus in most cases, necessitating lifelong therapy. 28. Antiviral drugs are not widely available or used in LMICs, leading to delayed intervention and advanced liver disease. 29. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines for the prevention, care, and treatment of CHB, complementing similar guidance for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. 30. These guidelines prioritize simple, non-invasive diagnostic tests to assess liver disease stage and treatment eligibility, recommend treatment for those with advanced liver disease, and advocate for the use of nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high barrier to drug resistance (e.g., tenofovir and entecavir) for firstand second-line therapy. 31. Lifelong treatment is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis, along with regular monitoring for disease progression, drug toxicity, and early detection of HCC. 32. Special considerations are highlighted for specific populations, including those co-infected with HIV, HCV, or hepatitis D virus (HDV), as well as children, adolescents, and pregnant women. 33. Recommendations for HBV/HIV co-infected individuals are based on WHO’s 2013 guidelines on antiretroviral therapy, which will be updated in 2015. 34. The use of interferon or pegylated interferon was excluded from these guidelines due to high costs and significant adverse effects requiring careful monitoring, making them less feasible in LMICs. 35. Existing WHO recommendations for preventing HBV transmission include infant vaccination, catch-up vaccination for key populations, and prevention strategies for healthcare settings. 36. Alcohol reduction interventions are emphasized to slow liver disease progression in individuals with CHB. 37. Future guidelines will address hepatitis B and C testing algorithms, updated HCV treatment recommendations, and management of acute hepatitis B and C, as well as advanced liver disease. 38. Operational guidance will be needed to improve retention in care, adherence to antiviral therapy, and integration with other health services, such as maternal and child health clinics, tuberculosis clinics, and HIV services. 39. The development of these guidelines followed WHO’s established procedures, with recommendations formulated using the GRADE approach, which considers evidence quality, benefits and harms, patient values, resource use, and feasibility. 40. Most evidence was derived from studies in adults from Asia, North America, and Western Europe, with limited data from sub-Saharan Africa and children. 41. These guidelines aim to save lives, improve clinical outcomes, reduce HBV incidence and transmission, and address stigma, while posing practical challenges for policymakers and implementers in LMICs. 42. Implementation considerations include decision-making and planning for hepatitis treatment programs, taking into account HBV epidemiology, health system capacity, laboratory services, drug supply systems, financial resources, and ethical and human rights considerations. 43. Particular challenges exist in implementing lifelong care and treatment programs for CHB in LMICs, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, where access to diagnostic assays, antiviral therapies, and appropriate infrastructure is limited.
